content: \chaplabel{binarytrees} This chapter introduces one of the most fundamental structures in computer science: binary trees. The use of the word \emph{tree} \index{tree} \index{tree!binary} \index{binary tree} here comes from the fact that, when we draw them, the resultant drawing often resembles the trees found in a forest. There are many ways of ways of defining binary trees. Mathematically, a \emph{binary tree} is a connected, undirected, finite graph with no cycles, and no vertex of degree greater than three. For most computer science applications, binary trees are \emph{rooted:} \index{tree!rooted} \index{rooted tree} A special node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}, of degree at most two is called the \emph{root} of the tree. For every node, $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}\neq \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}$, the second node on the path from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} is called the \emph{parent} of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}. \index{parent} Each of the other nodes adjacent to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} is called a \emph{child} \index{child} of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}. Most of the binary trees we are interested in are \emph{ordered}, \index{ordered tree} \index{tree!ordered} so we distinguish between the \emph{left child} and \emph{right child} of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}. \index{left child} \index{child!left} \index{right child} \index{child!right} In illustrations, binary trees are usually drawn from the root downward, with the root at the top of the drawing and the left and right children respectively given by left and right positions in the drawing (\figref{bintree-orientation}). For example, \figref{binary-tree}.a shows a binary tree with nine nodes.

content: Because binary trees are so important, a certain terminology has developed for them: The \emph{depth} \index{depth} of a node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, in a binary tree is the length of the path from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} to the root of the tree. If a node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}, is on the path from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}, then \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}} is called an \emph{ancestor} \index{ancestor} of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} a \emph{descendant} \index{descendant} of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}. The \emph{subtree} of a node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, is the binary tree that is rooted at \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} and contains all of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}'s descendants. The \emph{height} \index{height!in a tree} of a node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, is the length of the longest path from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} to one of its descendants. The \emph{height} of \index{height!of a tree} a tree is the height of its root. A node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, is a \emph{leaf} \index{leaf} if it has no children. We sometimes think of the tree as being augmented with \emph{external nodes}. Any node that does not have a left child has an external node as its left child, and, correspondingly, any node that does not have a right child has an external node as its right child (see \figref{binary-tree}.b). It is easy to verify, by induction, that a binary tree with $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\ge 1$ real nodes has $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}+1$ external nodes.

content: Using recursion this way produces very short, simple code, but it can also be problematic. The maximum depth of the recursion is given by the maximum depth of a node in the binary tree, i.e., the tree's height. If the height of the tree is very large, then this recursion could very well use more stack space than is available, causing a crash. To traverse a binary tree without recursion, you can use an algorithm that relies on where it came from to determine where it will go next. See \figref{bintree-traverse}. If we arrive at a node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{parent}}}}, then the next thing to do is to visit \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{left}}}}. If we arrive at \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{left}}}}, then the next thing to do is to visit \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{right}}}}. If we arrive at \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{right}}}}, then we are done visiting \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}'s subtree, and so we return to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{parent}}}}. content: To add a new value, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}, to a BinarySearchTree, we first search for \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}. If we find it, then there is no need to insert it. Otherwise, we store \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} at a leaf child of the last node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}}}, encountered during the search for \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}. Whether the new node is the left or right child of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}}} depends on the result of comparing \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{x}}}}.

content: Binary trees have been used to model relationships for thousands of years. One reason for this is that binary trees naturally model (pedigree) family trees. \index{family tree} \index{pedigree family tree} These are the family trees in which the root is a person, the left and right children are the person's parents, and so on, recursively. In more recent centuries binary trees have also been used to model species trees \index{species tree} in biology, where the leaves of the tree represent extant species and the internal nodes of the tree represent \emph{speciation events} \index{speciation event} in which two populations of a single species evolve into two separate species. Binary search trees appear to have been discovered independently by several groups in the 1950s \cite[Section~6.2.2]{k97v3}. Further references to specific kinds of binary search trees are provided in subsequent chapters. When implementing a binary tree from scratch, there are several design decisions to be made. One of these is the question of whether or not each node stores a pointer to its parent. If most of the operations simply follow a root-to-leaf path, then parent pointers are unnecessary, waste space, and are a potential source of coding errors. On the other hand, the lack of parent pointers means that tree traversals must be done recursively or with the use of an explicit stack. Some other methods (like inserting or deleting into some kinds of balanced binary search trees) are also complicated by the lack of parent pointers. Another design decision is concerned with how to store the parent, left child, and right child pointers at a node. In the implementation given here, these pointers are stored as separate variables. Another option is to store them in an array, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}}}, of length 3, so that \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[0]}} is the left child of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[1]}} is the right child of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}, and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[2]}} is the parent of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}. Using an array this way means that some sequences of \ensuremath{{\color{black} \textbf{if}}} statements can be simplified into algebraic expressions. An example of such a simplification occurs during tree traversal. If a traversal arrives at a node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} from \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}]}}, then the next node in the traversal is $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}}}[(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}+1)\bmod 3]$. Similar examples occur when there is left-right symmetry. For example, the sibling of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}]}} is $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}}}[(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}+1)\bmod 2]$. This trick works whether \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{p}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}]}} is a left child ($\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}=0$) or a right child ($\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{i}}}}=1$) of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}. In some cases this means that some complicated code that would otherwise need to have both a left version and right version can be written only once. See the methods \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{rotate\_left}(\ensuremath{\mathit{u}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{rotate\_right}(\ensuremath{\mathit{u}})}} on page~\pageref{page:rotations} for an example.

visits \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} after visiting all the nodes in \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}'s left subtree but before
visiting any of the nodes in \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}'s right subtree.  A \emph{post-order}
traversal visits \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} only after visiting all other nodes in \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}'s subtree.
The pre/in/post-order numbering of a tree labels the nodes of a tree with
the integers $0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}-1$ in the order that they are encountered
by a pre/in/post-order traversal.  See \figref{binarytree-numbering}
for an example.
